MORE CAFE PARISIEN
EVIDENCE.

label: text
text: Conflicting evidence was given yesterday at the Magistracy in the case in which Mr. L. G. Taylor, manager, and Mr. J. L. Durand, part proprietor, are charged with disorderly conduct. The case was adjourned until Monday afternoon.

label: text
text: CONFLICTING VERSIONS.

label: text
text: Mrs. Taylor, describing the events of July 14, when the incidents on which the charges are based are alleged to have taken place, said that Madame Flint told her she was no good and that she wasn't wanted there. Witness demanded a formal letter of dismissal from Mr. Durand and he promised to give her one. Refering to the alleged attack by Mr. Durand on herself, witness said that Mr. Durand abused her and kicked her in the stomach. It was whilst Mr. Durand was upstairs drafting a letter of dismissal for herself and her husband that her husband came in. She acquainted him with what had transpired and he went upstairs to Mr. Durand.

label: text
text: Shortly after, Mr. Durand came rushing down the stairs, continued witness, and grabbed hold of her. His hands were bleeding and witness said the dress she had put in as an exhibit in the case showed the marks.

label: text
text: Questioned about the wine she had that night, Mrs. Taylor said she and her two companions had one bottle of champagne at dinner. She then went to the cinema, and on returning had another bottle of wine. Five people were present when that bottle was used.

label: text
text: Witness denied in cross-examination that she had boasted of having sold $200 of champagne on the night in question and complained that this fact didn't seem sufficiently appreciated.

label: text
text: Messrs. A. H. Rowe and C. Hugo were called by Mr. Hugh Jones (solicitor for Mr. Durand). They were among the guests dining at Mr. Durand's table on July 14, they stated. There were six people altogether but during the evening I've all others joined the party. T. lost of the drinks consumed the guests was defrayed by r. Durand who signed all the chi. He was not intoxicated.

label: text
text: Mr. Durand was called and in his evidence said that the letter on which he was engaged at the time when Mr. Taylor entered the room and struck him was not one of dismissal. It referred to a change in Mrs. Taylor's duties from the direction of the service bar to that of the linen. Mrs. Taylor had told him she wanted it in writing. In the course of Mr. Taylor's attack on him witness had his hand cut on a window, he stated.

label: text
text: Witness said he then went outside and saw a policeman. He was later asked to go to the police station. He asked for a chair and went peacefully. Witness denied assaulting Sergeant Hayward.

label: text
text: Continuing witness said: "I wanted to avoid any further trouble I did not want to catch him by the neck and break him to pieces, so I went down stairs and Mrs. Taylor attacked me again. Thinking that she would slap me I held out my hand. That explains the blood being on her clothes."

label: text
text: Witness also denied that prior to Mr. Taylor going "upstairs he had kicked Mrs. Taylor. " He was angry about some sailors being admitted after twelve o'clock and asked Mrs. Taylor where her husband was. Mrs. Taylor slapped him twice but he did not retaliate. He merely put one foot out and his hands in self defence.

label: text
text: The case will be resumed on Monday.

label: text
text: Claim Pending.

label: text
text: The case is down for hearing on Wednesday next and Mr. Vaux, solicitor for Mr. Durand, indicated that there would be a counter-claim as Mr. and Mrs. Taylor had left their employment without giving notice.

label: text
text: A case is pending in which Mr. and Mrs. Taylor claim from Mr. Durand in the Summary Court the sums of $975 and $988.12 respectively in respect of salaries and voyages to Hongkong and back from Shanghai.

label: text
text: Strangers.—Frank A. Munsey told a story about a feast that Jupiter gave to all the virtues. The virtues were very jolly and sociable at the feast, but two of them—two of the most beautiful of them—seemed stiff and constrained in each other's presence.

label: text
text: "Accordingly, Jupiter took the one virtue by the hand and led her to the other."

label: text
text: “'Benevolence,' he said—'your sister,' Gratitude."

label: text
text: “The two virtues were indeed astonished. This was the first time since the creation of the world that they had ever met.”

label: paragraph_title
text: STORM DAMAGE.

label: text
text:
ESTIMATED AT MILLION
DOLLARS.

label: text
text: YESTERDAY'S STATEMENT.

label: text
text: Although it was impossible to give exact figures at the moment of the damage the recent flood had caused in the Colony, said the Hon. Mr. W. T. Southorn; Colonial Secretary, at yesterday's meeting of the Finance Committee; it was anticipated that it would be in the neighbourhood of a million dollars.

label: text
text: As authority was needed for proceeding with the work of restoration it was proposed that a vote of $600,000 be passed at that meeting. A formal vote would be before the Committee at its next meeting when more accurate details would be available.

label: text
text: The tentative figures were.—Hongkong $510,000, Kowloon and New Kowloon $60,000 and New Territories $30,000, a total of six lakhs; but he was afraid they would not get off with that figure as it only represented what the P.W.D. thought they would want up to December 31.

label: text
text: The vote was approved.

label: text
text: All the votes, particulars of which were given yesterday, were approved. A mistake in the official figures was responsible for repair work on the Police launch No. 4 (which went aground) being given as $1,700. It was explained that the figure should be $17,000.

label: text
text: With regard to a vote of $75,000 for reclamation of Quarry Bay, Marine Lot No. 4, due to more expense being incurred than was anticipated in the construction of foundations to certain parts of the sea wall protecting the reclamation, the Hon. Mr. Creasy said the original contract was made prior to 1923 and the whole contract was considerably changed owing to an exchange with Messrs. Butterfield and Swire. It was connected with the 100 foot road at that point.

label: text
text: The Government took over from Messrs. Butterfield and Swire a row of buildings and in exchange they were to reclaim a part of Quarry Bay and put up a retaining wall to protect the reclamation. The work was still in progress. The original contract was a small one and the contractor failed in 1923 and when the Netherlands company arrived they took over the quarry from the contractor and used it for their block yard.

label: text
text: The Chairman: Do you think it will be completed for the $176,000?

label: text
text: The Hon. Mr. Creasy replied in the affirmative and went on to explain that the recent storms had damaged the wall to some extent.

label: paragraph_title
text: NEW WARSHIPS.

label: paragraph_title
text: EIGHT SPECIALIST OFFICERS APPOINTED

label: text
text: The principal British men-of-war, due to be completed during the current financial year are the battleships Nelson and Rodney, and in anticipation of their entry into service, about eight specialist officers have now been selected. These include for the Nelson Lieut.-Commander G. B. Middleton, who in 1923-25 was in the Hawkins, and Fleet Torpedo Officer for the China Station.

label: text
text: Submarine L.9, which has been paid off at Hongkong and placed on the disposal list for sale, is one of the 31 bouts of a similar type built under the emergency war programme of 1917-22.

label: text
text: These submarines, which are to be gradually eliminated from our underwater service, are improved or enlarged "E's" and generally follow the lines of that class; but, in addition to an increased number of torpedo tubes—four 21-inch bow tubes—they carry a 4-inch gun. The L.9 was built at Denny's, avian equipped with two sets of Diesel engines of 2,400 h.p., giving a surface speed of 17.5 knots, while the electrically driven machinery of 1,600 h.p. gave a submerged speed of 10.5 knots.

label: text
text: The L type gave the best result; of any submarine during the war period, their displacement of 1,070 tons making them more comfortable as sea boats than their pre-accessor.

label: text
text: After giving evidence in a case against himself, the senior accountant of the Cheong Kee money changer shop in Queen's Road Central was found "not guilty" yesterday by Mr. R. E. Lindsell. The charge was one of uttering two forged Hongkong and Shanghai Bank notes.

label: text
text: (Continued from Page 1.)

label: text
text: and that "this Hongkong severance of economic relations with Canton suggested the precise form in which patriotic retaliation for June 23 should express itself." This is a good example of putting a bad construction on perfectly innocent actions. The "Hongkong Government did not institute any blockade of Canton or the rest of the province. Hongkong did not sever economic relations with Canton. The prohibition of the exportation of certain foodstuffs was a measure dictated by common prudence for the purpose of conserving the food supplies of the Colony. By June 22 the shipping strike had already begun, and no one knew how far the importation of foodstuffs into the Colony might not be interfered with. If this was a blockade by Hongkong it was a blockade of the whole world. The object of the prohibition was to show by the notification of August 11, which announced that licences would be given freely for the exportation to all distinctions being subject to adequate reserves being maintained in the Colony, and the embargo was wholly removed on October 9. The prohibition of the exportation of coin, bullion and notes was a measure of ordinary financial prudence for the protection of the currency and financial system of the Colony. Thus, purely defensive measures, imposed on Hongkong by the strike, are twisted into an attack on Canton. In fact, the statement of the Chinese delegation on this point seems to be a desperate attempt to find an excuse and an explanation for the institution and maintenance of the boycott against Hongkong, a community which had not been concerned in any way with the incidents previously described.

label: paragraph_title
text: Indignant Protest.

label: text
text: Finally, we take this opportunity to enter an indignant protest against the attempt which has been made by means of unscrupulous propaganda throughout the course of this unhappy trouble to throw the blame on Hongkong and on the British nation. In truth, the malady of which the Chinese delegation speak is an internal one and will not be cured by attacking the British people, who of all others are most" desirous of seeing a happy, prosperous and independent China with whom they can conduct their trade.

label: text
text: We fully appreciate the fact that the whole outlook of large sections of the Chinese people has changed in recent years, and we sincerely sympathise with the ambition of the Chinese nation to take that great place in the world to which its genius entitles it. The Government of Hongkong, in particular, is prepared to assist in the development of these provinces with which the Colony is brought into immediate contact, in any way which may be of mutual benefit, and it is in this direction that we hope a solution of the present difficulties may be found.

label: text
text: [Canton's communique is published elsewhere in this issue. With regard to making known the Hongkong reply, it is interesting to note that one of the local vernacular papers, this morning, contains a translation of a part of the British communique—with a remark "to be continued"—which has obviously been culled from the Chinese papers in Canton. The conclusion is that the Hongkong reply has been handed out in Canton for publication but the vernacular papers there have only had time to translate the beginning of the statement.—Ed., "China Mail."

label: paragraph_title
text: A DEAR ROPE.

label: paragraph_title
text:
COSTS A COOLIE SIX MONTHS
IN JAIL

label: text
text: A coolie was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with robbery, by the local agents of the A.S. "Taiyo Maru."

label: text
text: An officer of the steamer testified that whilst the s.s. "Taiyo Maru" was tied to a buoy, the accused cut a line of rope which was hanging alongside the steamer for the guidance of all launches coming alongside. With as saw him cut the rope and ordered the quartermaster and the watchman of the steamer to arrest him.

label: text
text: Accused said that he was working on board the "Taiyo Mru" and that the rope belonged to him.

label: text
text: The Magistrate, Major William did not believe his story and sentenced him to six months' hard labour.

label: paragraph_title
text: JUST PAINT

label: text
text: DODGE TO EVADE CHINESE AND MALAY PIRATES.

label: text
text:
As the centuries slip by the part played by paint in a vessel's appearance steadily diminishes. The Tudor warships were absolutely dazzling in their paint and gilt work and the humbler merchantmen were made as festive as stern commercialism would allow. Even in recent years it was customary to go to some trouble and expense to paint on the sides of a ship a white streak with squares of black to represent gun ports, which gave them, as instance the "Loch Torridon," a very handsome appearance. One reason why this originally was done is said to have been that they appeared at a distance as men-of-war and therefore were let alone by Chinese and Malay pirates.
But to-day the warship has been made as invisible as possible, and economy has resulted in much the same standardisation for the Mercantile Marine, the funnels being the only remaining space where the colour artist is given

label: text
text: There are two well-known exceptions to the prevalent black hulls, namely, the Aberdeen White Star and the Union-Castle. The former still cling to the sea green, similar to what their famous clipper Thermopylae was painted, while the Union-Castle ships are easily recognisable by their slate coloured hulls.

label: text
text: Most companies favour white for deckwork, but the Peninsular and Oriental and the Nippon Yusen Kaisha have buff, which colour is selected as it is more durable and considerably less tiresome to the eyes under the intense tropical glare.

label: paragraph_title
text: STRIKES.

label: paragraph_title
text: FORTY IN SHANGHAI LAST MONTH.

label: text
text: There were forty strikes during June, which is the highest number ever recorded in a month in normal times. A desire on the part of the workers affected to show their sympathy with other members of their trade who were on strike accounted for thirteen of these disputes, economic discontent was the pretext put forward for thirteen more of them, and various forms of internal friction produced the remaining fourteen. The employees affected comprised 23,138 cotton mill workers, 23,920 silk flature operatives, 2,910 hemp sack factory employees, 1,150 Chinese and foreign-style tailors, 600 leather goods workers, 560 tobacco factory employees, 300 engineers and mechanics, 200 transport workers and 528 members of miscellaneous other trades. The strikes resulted in a loss of 71,233 days labour to co-creams in the Settlement, and 97,850 days to establishments in Chinese territory. Considerable loss also resulted from sabotage of which three cases occurred in the Settlement. The disputes furthermore involved a great amount of extra work for the Municipal Police who, in all cases, were obliged to make special arrangements for the maintenance of law and order.

label: text
text: It was remarked that the strikes in the Settlement occurred in areas close to Chinese territory where the vast majority of the workers affected have their homes.
